v.q: Why can't a transfer spanning two microservices use a single database transaction?
o: Each service owns its database, so no local transaction covers both
Databases refuse to commit more than one table
Microservices are not able to connect to databases
Transactions only work inside the browser
v.w: Distributed two-phase commit is possible but blocks and scales poorly. Sagas coordinate a sequence of local transactions instead.

v.q: Which option is NOT a way to keep money consistent across two services?
o: A single shared transaction
A saga with compensations
An orchestrator
Event-driven choreography
v.w: Each service owns its database, so no single local transaction covers both.

o: Local transactions in sequence, each with a compensating action
One big distributed lock across all services
A cache that survives restarts of the service
A retry loop that keeps no state at all
v.w: If step N fails, previously completed steps are undone by compensations, giving eventual consistency rather than atomicity.

v.q: Which statement about a saga is NOT true?
o: It gives full isolation like one ACID transaction
It is a sequence of local transactions
Steps have compensations
It is eventually consistent
v.w: Intermediate states are visible, so a saga needs countermeasures such as semantic locks.

v.q: A saga debited the source account, then crediting the destination failed. What does the saga do?
o: A compensating action credits the source account back
The first service's database transaction is rolled back
The failure is ignored and retried for ever
The debit record is deleted from the log
v.w: The first step already committed, so it cannot be rolled back. A new business action (the compensation) reverses its effect.

v.q: Which action undoes a completed credit step in a saga?
o: A compensating debit
A database rollback
Deleting the log
Restarting the service
v.w: The step is already committed, so a new action reverses its effect.

v.q: What is the difference between choreography and orchestration?
o: Choreography: services react to events. Orchestration: a coordinator steers
Choreography relies on a database, orchestration relies on a queue
Orchestration has no way of handling failures in a step
They differ only in which programming language is used
v.w: Choreography is decentralised but hard to follow as it grows. Orchestration gives one place to see and change the flow, at the cost of a coordinator.

v.q: Which style has a central component that tells each service what to do next?
o: Orchestration
Choreography
Sharding
Caching
v.w: An orchestrator sends commands and tracks state. In choreography each service reacts to events.

v.q: Why must saga steps and compensations be idempotent?
o: Messages can arrive twice, and a repeat must not repeat the effect
Compensations are guaranteed to run only a single time
Idempotent steps are simply quicker to execute than others
The database itself refuses writes that are not idempotent
v.w: At-least-once messaging plus retries means duplicates are normal. Track a saga id and step state so a repeat is ignored.

v.q: Which statement about saga steps is NOT true?
o: Running a step twice is harmless
Steps should be idempotent
Compensations should be idempotent
Messages may arrive more than once
v.w: Duplicates happen, so steps must handle a repeat without a second effect.

v.q: Which saga steps cannot simply be compensated, such as sending an email to a customer?
o: Steps with outside effects, so place them last or correct them afterwards
Steps that only read data and never change anything
Steps that write rows into a database of their own
Steps that stay entirely inside the boundary of one service
v.w: Order steps so that hard-to-undo actions run after the risky ones. Where undo is impossible, send a correcting follow-up instead.

v.q: Which step is hard to compensate?
o: Sending an email
Writing a database row
Reserving stock
Creating a pending order
v.w: An email cannot be taken back, so send it after the other steps succeed.

v.q: Which isolation problem do sagas introduce that a single ACID transaction avoids?
o: Others can see intermediate results before the saga completes
Writes become noticeably slower than reads in every service
Rows stay locked for the whole duration of the saga
Data ends up being encrypted twice on its way through
v.w: Countermeasures include semantic locks (a PENDING state), commutative updates and re-reading values before acting.

v.q: Which countermeasure reduces the visibility of intermediate saga states?
o: A PENDING status flag
A bigger database server
More retries on failure
A shorter network timeout
v.w: A semantic lock such as PENDING tells other flows that the record is still changing.

v.q: How does the transactional outbox help a saga participant?
o: It stores the outgoing event in the same local transaction
It removes the need for compensating steps
It makes the network itself reliable
It runs the whole saga on a single database
v.w: Without it the service could update its database and crash before publishing the event, leaving the saga stuck.

v.q: Which claim about an outbox in a saga step is NOT true?
o: It publishes the event before the commit
It writes the event with the data
A relay sends the event later
Consumers must handle duplicates
v.w: The event is saved in the same transaction and published after it, so no crash separates the two.
